patterns.name: Instant change
patterns.what: The change happens at once, with no animation.
useWhen: The action is repeated a hundred times a day or more: a keyboard shortcut, the command palette, moving through a list
The action is started from the keyboard
The screen is dense with data that the person is reading or acting on
No purpose can be named for a motion: feedback, where something came from, what changed
avoidWhen: Content appears or disappears so abruptly that people lose track of what changed (bridge it with a short fade)
A press gets no visible answer at all (give it press feedback)
rules: Show the new state within 100 ms of the action; an instant change that arrives late is worse than an animated one.
Keep the feedback that does not move: hover, focus, pressed and selected styles still change, at once.
When the choice is between a subtle motion and none on something used all day, choose none.

examples.where: You Don't Need Animations: a menu and a list shown with and without animation, and why the one used hundreds of times a day should have none
The command window opens and closes with no animation

motion.reduced: Nothing to reduce: nothing moves.

patterns.name: Press feedback
patterns.what: A button shrinks slightly while it is pressed and returns when it is released.
useWhen: A press has no visible answer of its own
The control is a button, card or tile that is tapped or clicked, on touch screens above all
avoidWhen: The control is pressed many times in a row, such as a stepper or a key of a keypad (change its color instead)
The control is a text link inside a sentence
The element is large: scaling a whole row or panel by 3% moves its edges visibly
rules: Scale to between 0.96 and 0.98; below that it reads as a bounce, not a press.
Take 100–160 ms with an ease-out curve, so the answer starts with the press.
Animate transform only; never width, height or padding.
Keep the pressed color or shadow as well, so the state does not rest on movement alone.
Under reduced motion drop the scale and keep the color change.

examples.where: 7 Practical Animation Tips: a button that scales to 0.97 while it is pressed

sources.where: Executing UX Animations: Duration and Motion Characteristics

motion.reduced: No scale; the pressed color still changes.

patterns.name: Hold to confirm
patterns.what: A button that must be held down while a fill runs across it; letting go early cancels.
useWhen: The action cannot be undone and a slip would be costly: delete for good, publish, send to everyone
A confirmation dialog would interrupt a flow that people repeat
avoidWhen: The action can be undone (offer undo instead)
The action is frequent; holding slows people down on purpose
No other way is offered to people who use a keyboard, a switch or voice
rules: Fill from the leading edge at constant speed over 1 to 2 seconds, so the time left can be read from the fill.
On release before the end, run the fill back in about 200 ms and do nothing.
Say what to do in the label: "Hold to delete".
Give keyboard and assistive-technology users another way: Enter or Space opens a confirmation instead.
When the hold completes, show the result in the button: the label changes to what happened.
The fill stays under reduced motion: it is progress, not decoration.

examples.where: Hold to publish: holding fills the pill from the left; letting go early sends the fill back
Hold button

sources.where: Never Use a Warning When you Mean Undo

motion.reduced: The fill while holding stays, because it shows how long to hold; it goes back at once instead of running back.

patterns.name: Hover lift
patterns.what: A card or tile rises a few pixels and its shadow deepens while the pointer is over it.
useWhen: The whole card is one link or button and little else says so
People browse a grid of cards on a marketing page, a catalog or a gallery
avoidWhen: Rows of a dense table or list that the pointer crosses all the time
The card is not clickable; a lift promises an action
It would be the only sign that the card can be clicked: touch screens have no hover
rules: Move 2–4 px up and deepen the shadow; do not scale the card, which blurs its text.
150–200 ms with an ease-out curve on the way in; the same or faster on the way out.
Apply it only where hover exists: @media (hover: hover) and (pointer: fine).
Show the same emphasis on keyboard focus, together with a visible focus ring.
Under reduced motion keep the shadow or border change and drop the movement.

examples.where: Fan cards: each card lifts and grows a little while the pointer is over it
Cards: an elevated card rises one level while hovered

motion.reduced: The shadow still deepens; the card does not move.

patterns.name: Icon swap
patterns.what: An icon changes into another at the moment its state changes: copy becomes a check, an outlined heart fills.
useWhen: A small action finishes at once and the control itself can say so: copy, like, save, mute
A toast would be too much for the action
avoidWhen: The result needs words, a link or an undo (use an inline confirmation or a toast)
The action can fail; an icon alone cannot explain an error
rules: The old icon fades and shrinks out while the new one fades and grows in, in 150–200 ms; both sit in the same box, so the control keeps its size.
Start the new icon from a scale of 0.8 or more, never from 0.
Change the accessible name or announce the result in a live region as well; the icon alone is not a message.
Return to the first icon after about 2 seconds if the state is momentary, such as Copied.
Under reduced motion swap by opacity only.

examples.where: Copy button: the copy icon shrinks away while a check pops in and the word changes to Copied
Like burst: the heart squashes, bounces up and fills

motion.reduced: The icons swap with a fade and do not change size.

patterns.name: Button status
patterns.what: A button shows the progress and the result of its own action in place: the label gives way to a spinner, then to a check and a word such as Sent.
useWhen: The action takes between about one and ten seconds and the page stays where it is
The button is where people look while they wait: send, save, pay, subscribe
avoidWhen: The action finishes at once (use an icon swap, or nothing)
The result leads to another page (use a confirmation page)
An error needs explaining; put the message next to the field or in a summary
rules: Keep the button's width, or change it once and smoothly; a button that jumps under the pointer invites a second click.
Disable the button while it works and say so to assistive technology: aria-busy, and the result in a live region.
Swap label, spinner and check with a 150–200 ms crossfade and a move of a few pixels; nothing longer.
Show the result for about 2 seconds, then return to the label or to the next state.
On failure return to the label at once and show the error beside the form.
Under reduced motion crossfade only; the spinner may still turn, because it reports progress.

examples.where: Loading to success: the label drops away, the button closes around a spinner, then opens with a check and the word Sent

motion.reduced: Label, spinner and result swap with a fade and do not move.

patterns.name: Sliding indicator
patterns.what: The highlight behind the selected tab or segment glides to the newly selected one instead of jumping.
useWhen: Tabs, a segmented control or a navigation bar with one highlight that marks the current item
The items sit in one row or one column, so the highlight has a path to travel
avoidWhen: Selection is changed from the keyboard all day, as in a list of mail or files (move it at once)
The items wrap onto several lines; the highlight would fly across the text
Each tab loads a new page; the highlight would start over on arrival
rules: Move one highlight element with transform; do not fade one out and another in.
200–250 ms with an ease-in-out curve: it starts and ends on screen.
The content below may crossfade; it does not slide unless the tabs are pages that swipe.
The selected state is also carried by weight, color and aria-selected, never by the highlight alone.
When selection changes with the arrow keys, follow at once.
Under reduced motion the highlight jumps.

examples.where: Tab pill: the highlight stretches toward the new tab and then pulls its tail in
Segmented control: the highlight rides to the chosen segment
Smooth tab

motion.reduced: The highlight jumps to the new item.

patterns.name: Crossfade
patterns.what: The old content fades out while the new content fades in, in the same place.
useWhen: Content is replaced in place and both versions occupy the same box: a tab panel, a picture, a label
A hard cut makes people miss that something changed
avoidWhen: The two versions differ in size, so the box jumps under the fade (animate the size too, or cut)
The switch is made from the keyboard all the time
There is a place to show: where a panel came from or went to
rules: 150–200 ms in total; longer reads as lag.
Change opacity only, and keep both versions in the same grid cell so the layout does not move.
Fade the old version out faster than the new one comes in, so both are never readable at once.
Take the old content out of the tab order and the accessibility tree as soon as it starts to fade.
A short fade is not movement: it may stay under reduced motion.

examples.where: Transitions: between top-level destinations the outgoing screen fades out before the incoming one fades in
Motion: top-level transitions

sources.where: Executing UX Animations: Duration and Motion Characteristics

motion.reduced: Stays as it is: a short fade is not movement.

patterns.name: Fade in
patterns.what: Something appears by going from transparent to opaque, without moving.
useWhen: A small element appears near where the person is looking: a tooltip, a hint, an inline message
Movement would be too much for how often it appears
Reduced motion is asked for and an entrance still needs a bridge
avoidWhen: The element comes from somewhere worth showing: a menu from its button, a drawer from an edge
It appears on a keyboard shortcut used all day
rules: 100–200 ms with an ease-out curve.
Fade out faster than in, or cut on the way out.
Do not delay it: the fade begins with the action.
Opacity is the only property that changes.
@starting-style gives an entrance to an element that was just added or just shown; where it is not supported the element simply appears.

examples.where: Motion: fades are micro-interactions and get the 110 ms duration token

sources.where: Executing UX Animations: Duration and Motion Characteristics

motion.reduced: Stays as it is: a short fade is not movement.

patterns.name: Grow from the trigger
patterns.what: A menu, popover or tooltip grows out of the control that opened it while it fades in.
useWhen: A small overlay opens from a button, field or icon: a dropdown menu, a popover, a select, a tooltip
Showing where it came from helps people find the way back
avoidWhen: The overlay is centered on the screen, such as a dialog: it has no origin, so it fades and grows from its own center
It opens on a keyboard shortcut used constantly
It is a tooltip shown right after another one of the same group (show it at once)
rules: Set transform-origin to the side of the overlay that touches its trigger, not to the center.
Start from a scale of 0.95–0.97 and opacity 0; never from 0.
125–200 ms with an ease-out curve for small popovers, up to 250 ms for menus and selects.
Close faster than it opens, or at once.
Under reduced motion fade only.

examples.where: 7 Practical Animation Tips: a popover that grows from the button that opened it, next to one that grows from its center
Morph tooltip: the first hover pops the tooltip in at its tool

sources.where: Executing UX Animations: Duration and Motion Characteristics

motion.reduced: The overlay fades in and does not grow.

patterns.name: Slide in from the edge
patterns.what: A drawer, sheet or toast slides in from the edge it belongs to and leaves through the same edge.
useWhen: A panel belongs to an edge of the window: a side sheet, a navigation drawer, a bottom sheet
A toast or notification arrives at the corner where toasts stack
avoidWhen: The surface is centered (fade it, and grow it from its center)
The panel is toggled all the time, like a sidebar collapsed with a shortcut (resize it at once)
rules: Enter and leave through the same edge; the direction tells people where it lives and how to dismiss it.
200–300 ms for sheets on desktop, up to 500 ms for full-height sheets on phones; ease-out on the way in, a little faster on the way out.
Move with transform, not with left, right or width.
Dim the page behind a modal sheet with a fade of the same duration.
Move focus into the panel when it has arrived, and back to the trigger when it has left.
Under reduced motion fade it in place.

examples.where: The Role of Animation and Motion in UX: a navigation menu that slides over the page when the menu icon is tapped
Motion: toasts and system communication get the 240 ms duration token

motion.reduced: The panel fades in where it will stand.

patterns.name: Expand in place
patterns.what: A section opens by growing to the height of its content, pushing what is below it down smoothly.
useWhen: An accordion, an FAQ answer, a details block or "Show more" opens in place
What is below would otherwise jump, and people would lose their place
avoidWhen: The content is very tall; a long travel is slow and the eye cannot follow it (open at once and keep the heading in view)
Many sections are opened in a row from the keyboard
rules: Animate between zero and the content's own height: grid-template-rows from 0fr to 1fr, or, on a native details element, interpolate-size with ::details-content where the browser supports them (elsewhere it opens at once). Never animate to a guessed max-height.
200–300 ms with an ease-out curve; fade the content in over the same time.
Close a little faster than it opens.
Turn the chevron, or change plus to minus, in the same time, as one movement.
The heading stays where it is; only what is below it moves.
Under reduced motion open at once; the content may fade in.

examples.where: Animate to height: auto: transitions between a fixed length and the content's own size
Expand card: the chosen row grows to its full height while the others give way

sources.where: The Role of Animation and Motion in UX

motion.reduced: The section opens at once; its content fades in.

patterns.name: Rise in
patterns.what: An element appears by fading in while it moves up a few pixels into its place.
useWhen: A new item joins the page: a toast, a row added to a list, a message
A section or card appears on a page that people do not open all day
avoidWhen: Lists that update by themselves many times a minute
The element came from a particular place (grow it from its trigger, or slide it from its edge)
Text that people are already reading would move
rules: Travel 8–16 px; more reads as a slide and takes attention.
200–300 ms with an ease-out curve.
Animate opacity and transform only, so nothing around it is laid out again.
A new item in a list: make room first or at the same time, so its neighbours do not jump after the entrance.
Under reduced motion fade in place.

examples.where: The Role of Animation and Motion in UX: a shopping list in which the field for the next item fades in and slides into place
Dynamic menu: the links rise in when the menu opens

sources.where: Executing UX Animations: Duration and Motion Characteristics
How to create high-performance CSS animations

motion.reduced: The element fades in where it stands.

patterns.name: Staggered entrance
patterns.what: The items of a group appear one after another with a short delay between them, as a cascade.
useWhen: A group of like items appears together on a page seen now and then: the cards of a landing page, the links of an opened menu
The order of appearance should lead the eye from the first item to the last
avoidWhen: Pages opened many times a day; the wait repeats every time
Long lists: the last item would arrive late
Items that people want to click at once; nothing may be unclickable while it waits
rules: 30–80 ms between items and no more than about 500 ms from the first to the last; stop adding delay after the first six to eight items.
Every item uses the same short entrance: a fade and a rise of 8–12 px in 200–300 ms.
One cascade per view; several at once cancel each other.
Run it once, when the group first appears, not on every redraw or when it scrolls back into view.
The items are in the page and can be focused from the start; only their appearance waits.
Under reduced motion show all items at once, with a fade at most.

examples.where: Sidebar collapse: when the sidebar opens, each label starts a little later down the list, so the names read in like a cascade
Dynamic menu: the links rise in with a short stagger

motion.reduced: All items are shown at once.

patterns.name: Reveal on scroll
patterns.what: Sections fade and rise into place as they are scrolled into view.
useWhen: A long marketing or story page that is read once, from top to bottom
The reveal paces the story: one point per screen
avoidWhen: Product screens, documentation and anything that people scan or search
The page is visited again and again
Parallax or taking over the scroll would be needed to make it work
rules: Reveal each section once; do not hide it again when it leaves the screen.
A short travel (12–24 px) and a fade, finished by the time the section is well into view; reading must never wait for scrolling.
The content is in the document from the start and readable without the effect: where scroll-driven animation is not supported, or reduced motion is asked for, it is simply there.
No parallax and no scroll-jacking: the page scrolls at the speed of the person's hand.
At most one reveal per section, not one per paragraph.

examples.where: Product pages: sections fade into place as the page is scrolled

motion.reduced: Every section is simply there.

patterns.name: Attention pulse
patterns.what: A ring around a small dot pulses a few times to draw the eye to something new.
useWhen: Something changed outside the person's focus and they should notice it once: a new feature, a step that is waiting for them
A static badge would be missed
avoidWhen: More than one thing would pulse on the same screen
The thing is not new any more; a pulse that never stops is noise
Errors and warnings, which need words
rules: Pulse two or three times, then rest as a still dot; anything that moves for more than five seconds needs a way to stop it.
Animate the scale and opacity of a ring around a still dot, so the marker itself stays readable.
One pulsing element per view.
The news is also there as text: a label, a badge with a count, or an accessible name.
Under reduced motion show the still dot only.

examples.where: Product tours: a pulsing hotspot marks the element that a tip belongs to

motion.reduced: A still dot.

patterns.name: Rotating words
patterns.what: One word of a headline is replaced by the next of a short list, one after another.
useWhen: A landing-page headline has to name several audiences or uses, and one sentence fits them all
The page is visited rarely and the headline is its main message
avoidWhen: The headline must be understood at a glance: the word on screen may be the wrong one when people look
Product screens
The words differ much in length and the line would reflow
rules: Three to five words; each stays readable for at least two seconds.
Reserve the width of the longest word, so the rest of the line never moves.
Stop after one round and rest on the strongest word; it also pauses on hover and on keyboard focus, and movement that runs for more than five seconds needs a way to stop it.
Every word is in the page as text for search engines and assistive technology; the rotation is decoration.
Under reduced motion show the strongest word, still.

examples.where: Word roll: the last word of the line rolls up and out while the next one rolls in from below
Dynamic text

motion.reduced: The strongest word, still.

patterns.name: Marquee
patterns.what: A row of logos, quotes or tags moves sideways in a continuous loop.
useWhen: A landing page shows more logos or short quotes than fit in one row, and none is more important than the others
The strip is decoration that says "many", not content to be read
avoidWhen: People need to read, compare or click an item (use a grid, or a carousel with controls)
The row fits without moving
Product screens, and pages with other movement near it
rules: Move slowly and evenly, about 30–60 px per second, with the list repeated once so that the loop has no seam.
Pause on hover and on keyboard focus, and give it a visible pause control: it runs for more than five seconds.
Fade the two ends into the background, so items do not pop in at the edge.
Hide the repeated copy from assistive technology and from the tab order.
Under reduced motion show a still row that wraps.

examples.where: Marquee: rows of review cards that scroll in a loop and pause on hover

motion.reduced: A still row that wraps.

patterns.name: Page crossfade
patterns.what: Going from one page to the next, the old page fades into the new one instead of being replaced in a flash.
useWhen: A site of separate pages where navigation should feel continuous: marketing sites, documentation, catalogs
Header and navigation are the same on both pages, so only the content appears to change
avoidWhen: Pages take long to load; a fade cannot hide a wait and makes it feel longer
Navigation is constant and done from the keyboard, as in a mail client or an editor
rules: 150–250 ms: the browser's default crossfade or shorter. Do not slide whole pages on desktop.
Opt in on both pages with @view-transition { navigation: auto }; browsers without support navigate as before.
Parts that stay, such as the header or a sidebar, get their own view-transition-name so that they do not fade with the content.
Never hold the navigation back for the effect: the transition starts when the new page can be drawn.
Under reduced motion switch it off.

examples.where: Cross-document view transitions: two pages that opt in with the @view-transition rule

sources.where: Cross-document view transitions for multi-page applications
The Role of Animation and Motion in UX

motion.reduced: No transition: the page changes at once.

patterns.name: Shared element
patterns.what: An element that is on both pages, such as a thumbnail and its large picture, travels and resizes from its old place to its new one during navigation.
useWhen: A list or grid opens into a detail page, and one visible element is the same thing on both: a picture, a card, a title
People go back and forth between list and detail and should keep their place
avoidWhen: The two elements differ so much in shape or content that the morph distorts them
More than one or two elements would travel at once
Details are opened all the time from the keyboard
rules: Give the element the same view-transition-name on both pages, and give that name to one element per page only: in a list, the item being opened.
250–400 ms with an ease-in-out curve: it starts and ends on screen and travels far.
Everything else crossfades underneath; only the shared element moves.
The same morph runs backwards on Back.
Under reduced motion the pages change at once or crossfade.

examples.where: Transitions: container transform, in which a card grows into the screen it opens
Today: a card grows into the article it opens

sources.where: Cross-document view transitions for multi-page applications

motion.reduced: No morph: the page changes at once.
